summary: All eight displayed numbers match the generated results and use the intended ours+Anc and sex-specific Jaro-Winkler columns. The main defect is that the visible slide describes a substantially broader sample than the code analyzes; it also leaves the men's Jaro-Winkler aggregation ambiguous.

findings.title: The visible slide presents restricted estimates as covering all attached 1940 records with a death month
findings.what_the_code_does: The slide says only “1940 records attached to a FamilySearch family-tree profile with a death month.” The code first requires `namefrst!="" & namelast!="" & fs_namefrst!="" & fs_namelast!=""`, then defines men as `sex==1 & lower(gender)!="female" & ref_first!="" & ref_last!=""` and women as `sex==2 & lower(gender)!="male" & ref_first!=""`, retaining only `men | wom`. It also covers only the hard-coded 49-jurisdiction model universe. These restrictions appear in the LaTeX comment but not in the audience-visible slide.
findings.why_it_matters: The displayed Ns and agreement rates describe a selected human-complete, profile-name-usable, gender-compatible subset, not all attached records with a death month. In particular, the women’s first-name estimates condition on both human surname fields being present even though surnames are not scored. Omitting these restrictions overstates the population to which the comparison applies and obscures potentially consequential selection.
findings.how_to_check: Tabulate the successive sample sizes in `profile_names_build.do` after the human-complete restriction, profile linkage, gender filter, usable profile-name filter, and death-month filter; compare the final sex-specific counts with 27,334,035 and 23,365,543.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a concise visible qualifier such as “49-jurisdiction, human-complete linked sample; compatible profile gender and usable reference names,” with a footnote if space is tight. For women, explicitly note that the base sample still requires all four human name fields.

findings.title: The slide does not disclose that men’s Jaro-Winkler score is an arithmetic mean across two fields
findings.what_the_code_does: The table labels the measure only “Jaro-Winkler,” while the code computes men’s full-name value as `gen double jn_`s' = (jf_`s' + jl_`s')/2`. This is the mean of separately computed first-name and surname similarities, not Jaro-Winkler similarity of a concatenated full-name string or a requirement that both fields meet a threshold.
findings.why_it_matters: A reader cannot determine the estimand from the visible slide, and may interpret the men’s values as full-string similarity. That changes how 0.904 and 0.935 should be understood and compared with the women’s first-name-only scores.
findings.how_to_check: Compare the men’s displayed values with the `JW full name` columns in `MATCHING/results/profile_names_jw.md:11-13`, then compare the construction at `MATCHING/profile_names_jw.do:139` with the generic slide heading.
findings.suggested_fix: Relabel the heading or bullet as “Jaro-Winkler: men = mean of first-name and surname scores; women = first-name score.”

review_limits: No paper draft was supplied, so claims-vs-code review was limited to the target slide and its comments; broader paper claims could not be checked.
The underlying data were not available for inspection and the Stata pipeline was not rerun. Runtime results were assessed from source, the generated Markdown, and the supplied log.
The slide deck was not compiled because the review was read-only, so visual overflow or rendering problems were not tested.
